segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Saul approved of his killing. On that day a great persecution broke out against the assembly in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Devout men buried Stephen and made a great lamentation over him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Saul was ravaging the assembly: entering house after house, he dragged off both men and women and handed them over to prison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now those who had been scattered went from place to place announcing the good news of the word.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The crowds with one accord paid attention to what Philip was saying, as they heard him and saw the signs he was doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So there was great joy in that city.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a man named Simon had already been in the city for some time, practicing magic and astonishing the nation of Samaria, claiming to be someone great.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is the Power of God that is called Great.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They paid attention to him because for a long time he had astonished them with his magic arts.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when they believed Philip as he announced the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he stayed close to Philip; and seeing signs and great works of power taking place, he was astonished.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who went down and prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the Spirit had not yet fallen on any of them; they had only been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Give me this authority too, so that anyone I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “May your silver go with you to destruction, because you thought you could acquire the gift of God with money!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You have no part or share in this matter, for your heart is not straight before God.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So turn back from this wickedness of yours, and beg the Lord that the intent of your heart might perhaps be forgiven you.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of wrongdoing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You yourselves beg the Lord for me, so that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, when they had solemnly testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they made their way back to Jerusalem, announcing the good news to many villages of the Samaritans.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Get up and go toward the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is a wilderness road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he got up and went. And there was an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a high official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he was returning, sitting in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Spirit said to Philip,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Go over and stay close to this chariot.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Philip ran up and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you really understand what you are reading?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How could I, unless someone guides me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the passage of scripture he was reading was this:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: In his humiliation justice was taken away from him. Who will describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The eunuch spoke up and said to Philip,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I beg you, about whom does the prophet say this? About himself, or about someone else?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Philip opened his mouth and, beginning from this scripture, announced to him the good news of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were going along the road, they came to some water, and the eunuch said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, water! What prevents me from being baptized?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He ordered the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Philip, however, turned up at Azotus, and as he passed through he announced the good news to all the cities until he came to Caesarea.

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' everywhere so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

Here the word has the article and is a title, the anointed king Israel expected, not a name for Jesus. This translation uses 'Messiah' where the title is the point and 'Christ' where it works as a name, as in 'Jesus Christ' in verse 12. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

The Greek word is the same one that in the plural is usually rendered 'Gentiles'. In the singular it means a people as an ethnic or political unit, and this translation uses 'nation' for that sense. Luke is presenting the Samaritans as a distinct people.

notes.phrase: the Power of God that is called Great
notes.note: 'Power' could be used as a title for God or for a divine being, so the crowds are claiming that the supreme divine power is present in Simon, not merely that he is impressive. Exactly what Samaritans meant by the title is uncertain. Christian writers from the second century onward remembered Simon as someone his followers revered as divine.

Most translations have 'miracles' or 'mighty works'. The Greek is the plural of the word used for Simon in verse 10, and 'astonished' is the word used there for his effect on the crowds. The rendering keeps that echo: the man hailed as the great Power is himself astonished by great works of power.

The Greek noun can mean 'matter, affair' or 'word, message'. Most translations take it as the matter in hand, the giving of the Spirit. Since the same noun is used in this chapter for the gospel message (verses 4, 14, 25), Peter may instead be saying that Simon has no share 'in this message'. 'No part or share' echoes Old Testament language about having no allotted inheritance.

'Repent' is the established rendering, and most translations keep it as including a change of life. In current English it centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. 'Turn back' is used to convey that.

notes.phrase: the gall of bitterness and the bond of wrongdoing
notes.traditional: the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity
notes.note: Both phrases echo the Greek Old Testament. The first recalls the warning in Deuteronomy 29:18 about a root that grows up into gall and bitterness, an image for someone who turns away from God and poisons the community. The second recalls the 'bonds of injustice' in Isaiah 58:6. The Greek preposition could also mean that Simon is headed for this condition rather than already in it.

The Greek phrase literally refers to midday and can mean either 'toward the south' or 'at about noon'. Most translations take it as the direction, which suits the route from Jerusalem to Gaza. Some interpreters prefer 'at noon', which would make the command more striking, since travellers avoided the midday heat.

The Greek does not mark whether this sentence is the end of the angel's words or an aside by the narrator; it is taken here as the narrator's. The word means 'deserted, uninhabited' and grammatically could describe either the road or Gaza itself, since the old city had been destroyed, but most interpreters take it of the road.

'Ethiopia' in Greek usage was the kingdom on the Nile south of Egypt with its capital at Meroe, in what is now Sudan, not the modern country of Ethiopia. 'Candace' was understood by Greek and Roman writers as a dynastic title borne by the queens of that kingdom and not as a personal name. To Mediterranean readers this was the far southern edge of the known world.

Royal courts often employed castrated men in positions of trust. The word could occasionally be used loosely for a court official, but as 'high official' follows separately it is probably literal here. Deuteronomy 23:1 barred such men from the assembly of Israel, while Isaiah 56:3–5 promises eunuchs who hold to God's covenant a place in his house. Luke does not say whether this man was a convert to Judaism or a Gentile worshipper of Israel's God.

notes.phrase: justice was taken away from him
notes.note: The quotation is Isaiah 53:7–8 in the ancient Greek version, which differs from the Hebrew. The Greek says literally 'his judgment was taken away', which may mean he was denied a fair trial, as rendered here, or that the sentence against him was lifted. 'His generation' is likewise open: it may refer to his contemporaries, his descendants, or his origin.

notes.phrase: What prevents me from being baptized?
notes.traditional: verse 37 included: And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.
notes.note: Verse 37 is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not printed in the Greek text translated here, so the numbering passes from 36 to 38. In later manuscripts Philip answers, 'If you believe with all your heart, you may,' and the eunuch replies, 'I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.' The addition was already known in the late second century and probably reflects early baptismal practice, but scholars widely agree it was not part of Luke's text.

Recurs throughout the New Testament and is traditionally 'preach', which now suggests a sermon; it must be kept distinct from εὐαγγελίζομαι.

candidates.reason: The plural is rendered 'miracles', 'mighty works' or 'deeds of power' across translations, and a single decision would keep its link with the singular 'power' visible.
Translations waver between 'power' and 'authority', which blurs the distinction from δύναμις across the Gospels, Acts and the letters.
Rendered 'iniquity', 'unrighteousness', 'injustice' or 'wickedness' in different places, and its relation to the δίκαιος word group should be handled consistently.
